A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same adaptive question-generation framework and CAB benchmark. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material across substantial reformatting and appendix renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of nine LLMs on explicit and implicit CAB questions, bias-category analyses, and a comparison of two LLM judges.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original human-study results, transferability analyses, bootstrap estimates, and scoring-sensitivity results.

M1.justification: The hierarchical quota search, generate/replace/refine operations, filtering, counterfactual evaluation, and multiplicative fitness remain unchanged. Expanded pseudocode and newly disclosed mutation probabilities provide additional documentation without establishing a changed procedure.

E1.justification: v2 adds a human bias-rating task with 47 retained participants in Appendix E. The underlying English CAB coverage, three sensitive attributes, domains, and explicit/name-based question variants remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Appendix E adds human ratings as a comparison reference for the automated judge. The nine evaluated frontier models and the existing GPT-5-mini versus Claude-4-Sonnet judge comparison remain unchanged. Newly discussed benchmarks are not evaluated as additional baselines.

E3.justification: New protocols include stratified human surveys using summarized answers, three intended raters per item, attention checks, and participant filtering. Appendix J adds selection/evaluation threshold sweeps from 1.25 to 3 and scoring-component variations. These extend evaluation design without establishing revisions to the retained benchmark experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds human validation of the judge, generator-family transferability analysis, two threshold-sensitivity analyses, and fitness-component/weight ablations. The alternative-LLM judge comparison already appeared in v1 Appendix E and is retained in v2 Appendix H.

E5.justification: Table 2 introduces bootstrap standard deviations using 1,000 resamples, while Appendix E reports human-rater dispersion and plotted uncertainty. These are substantive additions to uncertainty reporting. The existing three-response sampling procedure is unchanged; bootstrap resampling does not establish additional independent benchmark runs.

E6.justification: New results include Table 2's model-by-attribute bias scores, human judgments on 352 items, transferability scores, and ranking-sensitivity findings. For example, Table 2 reports sex-bias means of 1.41 for GPT-5 and 1.95 for Qwen3-235B. The main explicit/implicit benchmark plots and findings are retained, so these additions do not demonstrate same-setting performance improvements.

T1.justification: Appendix C.1 adds mathematical conditions claiming when component values place fitness above or below the selection threshold. These claims were absent from v1 and extend its mathematical reasoning, although they do not consistently follow from Section 3.1's normalization. The underlying fitness and quota formulas are retained.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain adaptive counterfactual question generation, the human-filtered CAB benchmark, and comparative analysis of persistent LLM biases. The abstract and conclusion are rewritten, but the contribution scope and headline scientific claims remain substantially the same.

C2.justification: v2 newly qualifies name-based evaluation as measuring perceived attributes, discusses compression and lost nuances in human-rated summaries, and interprets transferability and sensitivity results. Appendices C.1 and J expand explanations of scoring-component failure modes. Existing English/US-context and judge-reliability limitations are retained and elaborated.

D1.justification: v2 adds mutation probabilities, token/API-cost accounting, human-study instructions, and the GPT-5.2 summarization prompt. Existing model configurations and code/data links remain. Documentation also loses information: Appendix L.3 omits Jinja conditional and loop directives visible in v1 Appendix G.3, reducing the completeness of the printed template.

R1.justification: Appendix D substantially expands positioning against earlier benchmarks through arguments about saturation, infilling and likelihood-based evaluation, multiple-choice-derived generation, proprietary data, and restricted domains. It adds discussion of COMPL-AI and OpenBBQ. Publication-year and venue updates for retained works are bibliographic changes rather than new research coverage.

P1.justification: v2 edits the abstract and conclusion, tightens existing prose, standardizes terminology, and separates pseudocode from implementation details. It integrates a robustness subsection and reorganizes appendix headings, while preserving the main narrative sequence and most existing explanatory text.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column proceedings layout. New tables and human-study, transferability, and sensitivity plots substantially expand the displays. v1 Figure 15 is split between v2 Figures 7 and 18; existing benchmark charts are retained and repositioned.

improvement.justification: Human ratings and transferability/sensitivity tests extend v1's validation beyond its alternative-LLM judge check, while study and cost disclosures improve auditability. These gains are limited by summary-based human judgments, Table 2's inconsistent treatment as bias versus fitness, conflicting threshold reasoning in Appendix C.1, and missing template directives. The added evidence supports a modest net improvement.
